Use this if you want to remove the `./cache` directory and everything inside it: `rm -rf ./cache` is the standard recursive forced deletion command in shell.[1]

## Script

A minimal shell script would be:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
rm -rf ./cache
```

This works because `rm -r` deletes directories recursively, and `-f` suppresses prompts and ignores missing files.[1]

## Safer version

If you want a slightly safer script that only deletes the directory when it exists, use:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
if [ -d "./cache" ]; then
  rm -rf "./cache"
fi
```

The `-d` test checks that `./cache` is a directory before attempting removal.[2]

## Important note

Be careful with `rm -rf` because it permanently deletes files and directories without moving them to trash.[1]

Use `mv` to rename `./.local` to `./bi` in a shell script. The `mv` command renames or moves files and directories by taking a source path and a destination path.[1]

## Script

```sh
#!/bin/sh
mv ./.local ./bi
```

This renames the hidden directory `.local` in the current directory to `bi`.[1]

## Safer version

```sh
#!/bin/sh
if [ -d "./.local" ]; then
  mv ./.local ./bi
fi
```

This version first checks whether `./.local` exists as a directory before renaming it.[1]

## Important note

If `./bi` already exists, `mv` may move `./.local` into `./bi` instead of replacing its name, depending on what `./bi` is.[1]
